title: Ramadan: the drummer
hook: a drummer walks the streets before dawn to wake people for suhur

segments.voice: Yesterday, the iftar cannon, one boom to tell a whole city the fast is over. Your line was the cannon at sunset. What did you take gladly, and without delay? Day one thousand forty-three.

Tap. Tap-tap. Tap. It's the dark hour before dawn in a Ramadan street, and the only sound is a small drum. A man walks under the balconies with a lantern and a stick, striking a little drum slung at his side. He stops at a door and calls a name. Not a general shout: a name. The son of the baker. The widow on the second floor. Upstairs, a light goes on. Then another. A child at a window waves, and he waves back without missing a beat. He walks on to the next street. Today's word is what people call him: musaharati.
screen: `A DRUM BEFORE DAWN.` → `HE CALLS YOU BY NAME.` → `ONE LIGHT, THEN ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the job. The musaharati, as he's called in Egypt, wakes people for suhur, the meal eaten in the dark before the fast begins at dawn. Other places have other names for the same work. Second, the chant. As he walks, he calls out lines inviting the sleeper to wake and to declare God one, and then he adds the names of the households. That last part is the heart of it. A whole street, known by name, woken one door at a time. Third, a waking call in Medina. Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tell that in the Prophet's own city, peace be upon him, Bilal used to call out while it was still night, so that sleepers would wake. The Prophet told the people that Bilal's call did not mean the fast had begun: keep eating and drinking until Ibn Umm Maktum calls, for he calls at dawn. Two voices, one to wake, one to mark the start. Fourth, the gentleness. Nobody wants to be shaken awake. The musaharati comes with rhythm, a lantern and your own name, and he's gone before you're cross. Today alarms and phones often do the job, yet in some neighborhoods the drummer still walks, and children still wait at the window for him. Look back at this week: the farthest mosque in Jerusalem; mosques of mud and wood, Djenné; mosques built today; your nearest mosque, and its qibla; then Ramadan, with its lanterns, its cannon, and now its drummer. Places, then nights.
screen: `HE WAKES THE STREET FOR SUHUR.` · `WAKE, SLEEPER, AND DECLARE GOD ONE.` · `BILAL CALLS BY NIGHT.` · `A RHYTHM, A LANTERN, YOUR NAME.` · then, large: `WAKE FOR SUHUR.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about how you wake people. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you wake, or someone you'll speak to first tomorrow: a child, a partner, a parent, a roommate, a colleague at the first meeting. How do you usually do it? A shout up the stairs? A text? Now try it the drummer's way, in your mind: a soft knock, their name said kindly, a little patience while they come round. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. If not, simply wish them a good morning before it comes. The bell holds the time.
Musaharati. The Ramadan drummer who walks the streets before dawn, calling each house by name to wake for suhur. Today's word.
Your line: wake for suhur. Tomorrow morning, wake someone gently, with their name and a little patience, the way the drummer would. Day one thousand forty-three.

howItsDone: In parts of Egypt and other Muslim-majority lands, a musaharati still walks the streets before dawn in Ramadan with a small drum, calling households by name to wake for suhur.

fork.setup: you're in Medina in Ramadan, eating before dawn. you hear Bilal's call ring out. what does the Prophet tell people to do?
options: stop eating at once; the fast has begun.
keep eating and drinking until Ibn Umm Maktum calls.
go back to sleep until the dawn prayer.
fork.reveal: Bilal called while it was still night. the Prophet said to keep eating until Ibn Umm Maktum called, for he called at dawn.

original.note: Arabic (Egyptian usage): the one who wakes people for suhur, the meal before dawn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quaint street performer.
what it means: the drummer who wakes each house by name for suhur in Ramadan.
what a scholar hears: a job some link to Medina, where Bilal called by night and Ibn Umm Maktum at dawn, so people knew when to eat and when to stop.

notes: Week end (days 1037–1043): the teach closes with a short look back at the week.
The musaharati's chant (e.g. 'ya na'im, wahhid ad-da'im', 'O sleeper, declare the Eternal One') is described, not quoted; confirm the description.
Bukhari 1918–1919 and 617 (Bilal calls at night; eat until Ibn Umm Maktum calls) paraphrased; confirm numbers and wording.

Editor pass: 'dead middle of the night' corrected to the hour before dawn (suhur time); 'the oldest waking call' superlative cut; the claim that Bilal's call was to wake sleepers is now sourced to Bukhari 621 (Ibn Mas'ud), added to sources, confirm number; 'because the street wants him' (an unsupported motive) replaced in the teach and the myth reveal.
Transliteration 'mi-sah-ha-RAA-ti' follows Egyptian pronunciation (mesaharati); the index spells it musaharati. Confirm.

Audit (2026-10-01): trapdoor called the musaharati 'an echo of Medina', an unsourced link stated as fact; now 'a job some link to Medina'. Bukhari 617, 621 and 1918–1919 numbers match the Bilal / Ibn Umm Maktum reports.
